options.C: Insuring, billing, and auditing
options.D: Prescribing, dispensing, and storing

explanation: Think of health financing as collecting funds (raising), putting them together to share risks (pooling), and paying for care (purchasing). You've got this!

question: How has the role of the workplace nurse changed over time?

options.A: It narrowed down to only treating minor cuts and dispensing simple pain relievers.
options.B: It shifted from basic first-aid treatment to comprehensive health promotion and hazard analysis.
options.C: It moved away from factory settings to focus exclusively on community pediatric care.
options.D: It stopped working with management and now only answers to labor unions.

explanation: Great job thinking about how nursing grows! While early industrial nurses mostly handled simple cuts and bruises, today's occupational health nurses focus on broad prevention, ergonomics, and keeping workers safe every day.

question: Why is it important to share evaluation results back with the community members?

options.A: It proves to them that health workers are superior planners
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future community meetings
options.C: It forces them to pay taxes for the healthcare they received
options.D: It maintains motivation and highlights areas for improvement

explanation: Brilliant! Giving feedback lets the community see the impact of their hard work, keeps them excited, and guides what needs fixing next.

question: During an emergency cesarean section, a surgeon tells the team to skip the safety timeout because every second counts. How should the circulating nurse respond?

options.A: Walk out of the operating room and abandon the patient entirely.
options.B: Advocate for patient safety and lead a quick, focused verification timeout.
options.C: Argue loudly with the surgeon and threaten physical violence.
options.D: Obey immediately and say nothing throughout the operation.

explanation: Nurses act as patient advocates and must ensure safety protocols like verification timeouts occur, even during high-stress emergencies. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T9#GNS312_U5_T9_h6)

question: Before giving an antibiotic, a nurse scans the patient's wristband and the drug barcode with a handheld scanner. What is this safety step called?

options.A: SBAR handoff reporting

options.C: Barcode medication administration
options.D: Root cause analysis

explanation: You nailed it! This clever tech lets us double-check patient identity and medications right at the bedside to keep things extra safe.

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team (doctors, nurses, physiotherapists) so important for patients with advanced disseminated sclerosis?

options.C: It eliminates the need for any ongoing medical drug therapy

question: Which ethical principle simply means a nurse or researcher must 'do no harm' to study participants?

options.A: Non-maleficence

options.D: Veracity

explanation: Well done! Non-maleficence is all about keeping patients safe and preventing any physical or emotional harm.

question: Why must a primary health care nurse rely heavily on clinical judgment rather than advanced diagnostic equipment?

options.A: Patients in rural communities refuse modern testing
options.B: Diagnostic machines are only kept in tertiary hospitals
options.C: Advanced diagnostic tools are rarely available in basic health posts
options.D: Physicians forbid nurses from using laboratory equipment

question: What do we call sketchy publishers that charge money to print articles quickly without doing real peer review?

options.A: Predatory journals

question: What is the main reason for placing a Word catheter after draining a Bartholin cyst?

options.C: To keep the new drainage opening open so a fresh duct can form

question: Why is strong social participation so helpful during a community health crisis?

options.A: Government officials will visit the town more often
options.B: Patients will no longer need to visit physical clinics
options.C: It automatically lowers the cost of imported medicines
options.D: Neighbors are more likely to cooperate and help each other

explanation: Exactly! When people trust and talk to each other, it's much easier to mobilize support and look out for vulnerable ones during emergencies.

question: What is the core problem happening inside the body during clinical shock?

options.A: Widespread inadequate cellular perfusion throughout the body
options.B: An excessive buildup of red blood cells inside the heart
options.C: A sudden and permanent drop in body temperature only
options.D: Local inflammation confined strictly to superficial skin veins

question: How does setting small, realistic goals during follow-up visits help the patient?

options.A: It ensures the nurse does not have to do any paperwork
options.B: It replaces the need for any professional medical treatment
options.C: It builds their confidence and encourages active participation in recovery

explanation: Achievable goals empower patients, making them feel capable and involved in managing their own health. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T5#GNS314_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason for a nurse to log every workplace injury?

options.A: To provide data for spotting workplace hazard patterns
options.B: To punish workers who report minor pain or discomfort
options.C: To help employers improve safety standards over time

question: Which classic body sign gives yellow fever its name?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Erythema
options.D: Pallor

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do right after using a surgical instrument at the bedside?

question: Why is a functional referral network important for big teaching hospitals?

options.A: It eliminates the need for community health nurses altogether

options.C: It prevents minor health issues from clogging up specialist care
options.D: It ensures that doctors only work half-day shifts

explanation: When primary clinics handle minor cases and only refer severe ones, tertiary hospitals can focus on complex medical conditions. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T16#GNS225_U3_T16_h1)

question: You see an elderly patient from a remote village showing muscle wasting and slow wound healing during the lean season. What should you suspect first?

options.A: Nutritional vulnerability caused by seasonal food availability limits

options.C: An acute allergic reaction to local agricultural crops

question: What is the main goal of active case finding by a community health nurse?

options.A: Collecting accurate financial data for the local government health department
options.B: Reducing the number of patients who visit the clinic for minor headaches
options.C: Finding infected individuals early before they develop severe illness or spread the disease
options.D: Punishing families who refuse to bring their children for routine immunizations

explanation: Active case finding involves going into the community to identify sick people early, allowing prompt treatment and halting further transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h6)

question: What makes a portal system different from normal blood circulation?

question: Why is the immediate postpartum period considered the most critical time for postnatal care checks?

question: What valve does blood pass through immediately after leaving the right ventricle?

question: Why is providing respite care so important for family caregivers?

options.B: It teaches the patient how to live independently without any help

explanation: You're doing fantastic! Respite care offers a much-needed breather so caregivers can rest, recharge, and protect their own health. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h6)

question: Which group makes up the primary target population for half-way houses?

question: What is considered the single most effective way to stop the spread of infections in a hospital?

options.A: Wearing heavy utility gloves all day

options.D: Changing bed linens every morning

question: Why does dangerously high pressure inside the skull cause changes in how a patient's pupils react?

question: A couple struggling to conceive asks for a simple change they can make first. What is the best initial nursing advice?

question: A nurse wants to study fatigue among emergency room nurses. After defining the topic and choosing the hospital, what is the next logical step?

question: How do patient satisfaction surveys help a home health agency improve its care?

question: What is the correct way to fix a writing mistake on a paper patient chart?

question: What is a major problem when writing infection control policies?

question: A patient tests positive for HIV at the clinic. What is your best immediate nursing action?

question: A patient arrives with active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). What kind of precautions should you set up right away?

question: Why is it vital to educate family members about the fluid chart when they are visiting?

question: Which serious infection can easily spread by sharing unsterilized blades during scarification?

question: Which of these is a chemical barrier part of our innate defense?

question: Why is priority setting necessary during community health planning?

options.B: Diseases always occur in isolation rather than in groups

question: Which of the following is NOT a focus area during a health inspection survey in an SNF?

question: Why do patients on chemotherapy often lose their hair and get mouth sores?

question: Which of these is a very common trigger that makes pregnancy nausea worse?

question: What is the primary focus of gerontology?

question: What is the main feature of a non-experimental research design?

question: What is a major benefit of using an epidural for pain relief during labor for a patient with sickle cell disease?

question: A patient is going home soon but needs a hospital bed and oxygen set up at their house. Who usually arranges this?

question: A patient with an arterial line suddenly shows a drop in blood pressure on the monitor. What should you do first?

question: Which germ is the main cause of tuberculosis (TB)?

question: What does an operating budget typically cover for a nursing unit?

question: How does blocking dopamine receptors help a patient taking a major tranquilizer?

options.C: It reduces hallucinations and disorganized thinking
options.D: It lowers high blood pressure instantly

explanation: Too much dopamine activity can trigger psychotic symptoms. Blocking those receptors helps bring the patient back to a calm, clear reality.

question: What is an asymptomatic carrier?

options.A: A host who harbors an infectious agent without showing illness but can still spread it
options.B: A patient who has completely recovered and has lifelong immunity to a virus
options.C: An environmental surface that holds bacteria without allowing them to multiply
options.D: An animal that serves as the final dead-end host for a dangerous parasite

explanation: An asymptomatic carrier feels totally fine and shows no signs of sickness, but they are secretly carrying and spreading the germ to others.

question: A patient asks you why he developed gout, considering he loves rich meals and has high blood pressure. How do you explain it simply?

options.A: He has a severe bacterial joint infection passed down through his family
options.B: His kidneys and diet are allowing uric acid to build up crystals in his joints
options.C: His body is manufacturing too many red blood cells instead of white cells
options.D: His blood pressure medication is creating calcium deposits in his bones

explanation: You nailed it! Risk factors like diet, blood pressure, and kidney function team up to let uric acid levels rise, leading to crystal deposits.

question: A patient is unresponsive, not breathing, and has no pulse after choking. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Place the patient in an upright sitting posture
options.B: Start chest compressions and prepare for CPR
options.C: Administer oral medication to lower blood pressure
options.D: Wait quietly for the laboratory test results

explanation: No pulse and no breathing means cardiac arrest. Jump straight into CPR to keep any remaining oxygen moving!

question: Why is economic stability so important when a community health nurse tries to lower disease rates?

options.A: Economic status is the only factor recorded on a hospital admission form
options.B: Government policies prevent nurses from treating poor patients
options.C: Poverty often limits access to clean water, good food, and proper sanitation
options.D: Wealthy neighborhoods never experience infectious disease outbreaks

explanation: Well reasoned! When people have a stable income, they can easily afford basic needs like safe water and good nutrition, which naturally keeps diseases away.

question: What is the key feature of appropriate technology in primary health care?

options.A: It relies entirely on uninterrupted electrical power grids
options.B: It requires a university degree to operate safely
options.C: It must be imported directly from advanced industrial nations
options.D: It is affordable, culturally acceptable, and easy to maintain locally

explanation: Appropriate technology must fit the local context, meaning it is affordable, sustainable, and accepted by the community. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T5#GNS124_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why do doctors start checking for fertility issues after just six months for women aged 35 and older?

options.A: To account for the faster decline in ovarian reserve and egg quality
options.B: Because older couples have more frequent sexual intercourse
options.C: To prevent the development of chronic pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Because hormonal treatments work much faster in older women

explanation: Spot on! Egg quality and quantity change faster as women get older, so catching things early helps. You are learning fast!

question: Why do nursing schools connect classroom lectures with clinical ward postings?

options.A: To help you apply what you read in textbooks to real patients
options.B: To cut down the number of hours you spend in school
options.C: To replace tests with chats by the patient's bedside
options.D: To keep students away from the school campus

explanation: Bridging theory and practice helps you understand the real 'why' behind the bedside care you give to your patients.

question: What kind of pain do adjuvant medications like gabapentin usually target?

options.A: Sudden high fever from bacterial infection
options.B: Acute inflammatory joint swelling
options.C: Neuropathic pain from damaged nerves
options.D: Severe stomach cramping from food poisoning

explanation: Gabapentin and similar drugs are originally seizure medicines, but they work wonders for that burning, shooting pain caused by damaged nerves.

question: Which everyday Nigerian kitchen item is a powerhouse source of Vitamin A?

options.A: Polished white rice
options.B: Red palm oil
options.C: Processed wheat flour
options.D: Refined white sugar

explanation: Well done! Unrefined red palm oil is loaded with beta-carotene, which our bodies turn straight into healthy Vitamin A.

question: When a psychiatric patient becomes aggressive in the ward, what should you try FIRST before considering physical restraints?

options.A: Discharging the patient immediately from the unit
options.B: Immediate solitary confinement in a locked room
options.C: Administering the highest legal dose of sedatives
options.D: Verbal de-escalation and calming the environment

explanation: Restraints are always an absolute last resort! Nurses should always try calm talk, a quiet space, and soothing body language first to help the patient feel safe.

question: Which layer of the skin is affected in a simple first-degree (superficial) burn?

options.A: Both epidermis and deep muscle
options.B: The epidermis only
options.C: The dermis and fat layer
options.D: Only the subcutaneous tissue

explanation: Great job! First-degree burns only touch the outer layer of skin (the epidermis), causing redness and mild pain without any blisters.

question: Which of these makes an infection show up much faster (shortens the incubation period)?

options.A: Strong baseline immunity in the host
options.B: Slow replication rate of the pathogen
options.C: A very high initial infectious dose
options.D: Superficial entry through intact skin

explanation: Correct! If a huge number of germs enter your body at once, they don't need as much time to multiply before making you sick.

question: You are managing a home birth, and the placenta won't come out after 45 minutes even with active management, while bleeding increases. What should you do?

options.A: Encourage the mother to stand up and walk around the room
options.B: Attempt manual removal of the placenta immediately using bare hands
options.C: Wait another hour because retained placenta is completely harmless
options.D: Initiate emergency transfer to a hospital while monitoring bleeding and vital signs

explanation: You made the right call. A retained placenta with extra bleeding is an emergency that needs quick hospital transfer to keep the mother safe.

question: Why should nursing students learn about health economics and GNP?

options.A: It equips them to advocate for better resource allocation and health policies
options.B: It removes all administrative duties from the daily nursing routine
options.C: It guarantees an automatic increase in hospital admission capacities
options.D: It allows them to personally invest in pharmaceutical manufacturing companies

explanation: Knowing how money and health connect helps you speak up confidently for better tools, fair pay, and policy changes for your patients.

question: Which white blood cell is the most common and acts as the quick-response team against bacteria?

options.A: Neutrophil
options.B: Eosinophil
options.C: Basophil
options.D: Lymphocyte

explanation: Well done! Neutrophils make up the biggest percentage of your white blood cells and are usually the very first heroes to arrive at a bacterial infection site.

question: Which group of people has a naturally higher risk for bone density loss and fractures?

options.A: Professional athletes
options.B: Active teenagers
options.C: Young children
options.D: Older adults

explanation: Aging naturally leads to a gradual reduction in bone density and muscle mass, increasing fracture risks. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T25#GNS222_U1_T25_h2)

question: What term is used to describe shortness of breath that occurs specifically when a patient lies flat?

options.A: Tachypnea
options.B: Apnea
options.C: Bradypnea
options.D: Orthopnea

explanation: Orthopnea is breathing difficulty that worsens when lying down and improves when sitting upright. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h2)

question: A 16-year-old mother is getting ready for discharge after delivery. What is a top priority for her discharge education?

options.A: Information on filing for adult emancipation
options.B: Dietary guidelines for managing geriatric menopause
options.C: Instruction on how to return to competitive sports immediately
options.D: Contraception counseling to prevent rapid repeat pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! Teenage mothers have a high chance of getting pregnant again too soon, so family planning guidance before discharge is vital.

question: How was the role of a nurse different in early asylum days compared to modern nursing?

options.A: Nurses focused exclusively on intensive individual psychotherapy
options.B: Nurses were primarily responsible for prescribing antipsychotic medications
options.C: Nurses spent most of their time running community outreach clinics
options.D: Nurses functioned mainly as guards focused on physical containment and order

explanation: Correct! Back then, security came before healing, so nurses spent a lot of their time managing locked doors and enforcing physical control instead of therapeutic care.

question: What term describes the study of what the body does to a drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion)?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics
options.B: Pharmacogenetics
options.C: Pharmacodynamics
options.D: Pharmaceutics

explanation: Nailed it! Pharmacokinetics tracks the journey of the drug through the body across those four famous ADME stages.

question: What is the main purpose of evaluating a public information campaign after a disaster drill?

options.A: To see if the messaging reached the audience and changed behavior
options.B: To increase advertising fees for local television stations
options.C: To punish individuals who failed to follow instructions
options.D: To replace all existing nursing personnel in the facility

explanation: You got it! Evaluating helps health planners see what worked well and what needs fixing for the future.

question: Why is it usually unhelpful to just blame an individual nurse when an error occurs?

options.A: It ignores the deeper system and workflow flaws that caused the error
options.B: Individual mistakes never actually lead to serious patient injuries
options.C: Nurses are protected by law from ever making mistakes
options.D: Blaming workers makes hospital administrators work much slower

explanation: Fixing bad workflows stops future mistakes. Just blaming a person doesn't change the unsafe conditions they had to work in.

question: A patient refuses birth control pills because she heard they cause permanent infertility. How should you reply?

options.A: Ignore her concern and write the prescription anyway
options.B: Explain that fertility returns quickly once pills are stopped
options.C: Tell her infertility is the price for effective protection
options.D: Agree with her and suggest only natural calendar tracking

explanation: Clearing up this myth reassures the patient that her body will be ready to conceive in the future whenever she chooses.

question: Why is it a bad safety practice for healthcare workers to recap used needles?

options.A: It is the leading cause of accidental needlestick injuries
options.B: It makes the needle too dull for future use
options.C: It contaminates the plastic barrel with air bubbles
options.D: It violates hospital rules regarding medication labeling

explanation: Trying to guide a used needle back into its tiny cap is the easiest way to slip and prick your own finger. Safety first—never recap!

question: When doing a community assessment, what does 'resource mapping' actually involve?

options.A: Counting how many patients die in the regional hospital
options.B: Listing roads that need paving by the federal government
options.C: Identifying local strengths, active groups, and facilities
options.D: Calculating the exact profit of local medicine shops

explanation: Resource mapping is like drawing a treasure map of your community's strengths—finding local groups, clinics, and assets that can help improve health.

question: Why must dangerous infections like cholera be reported immediately to health authorities?

options.A: To ensure the hospital receives full financial reimbursement.
options.B: To update international travel visa records automatically.
options.C: To trigger rapid outbreak containment and protect the community.
options.D: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on infected populations.

explanation: Spot on! Quick reporting lets public health teams jump into action, find the source, and stop an epidemic before it spreads.

question: Why should nurses always advise patients not to keep leftover antibiotics for later use?

options.A: It increases the financial profit of the hospital
options.B: It causes the plastic containers to lose their shape
options.C: It encourages drug resistance and improper self-medication
options.D: It makes the pharmacy run out of receipt paper

explanation: Incomplete doses are a major driver of antibiotic resistance. Patient education here saves lives down the line!

question: What is the name of the specific space that directly surrounds and protects the human heart?

options.A: cranial cavity
options.B: pleural cavity
options.C: pericardial cavity
options.D: mediastinum cavity

explanation: Think 'peri' for around and 'cardio' for heart! The pericardial cavity is the cozy, fluid-filled space right around your heart.

question: What is a major reason food gets lost before it ever reaches the local market?

options.A: Excessive consumer demand in urban centers
options.B: High levels of crop diversity on small farms
options.C: Poor storage facilities and bad transport roads
options.D: Strict government food safety inspections

explanation: Bad roads and poor storage mean a lot of harvest spoils before getting to people who need it. A very real challenge in many regions!

question: Why is carrying twins or triplets automatically tagged as a high-risk pregnancy?

options.A: The maternal body experiences much greater physiological strain.
options.B: The mother cannot produce breast milk after birth.
options.C: It always ends in a surgical delivery before 30 weeks.
options.D: Chromosomal abnormalities never happen in twins.

explanation: Brilliant! Carrying more than one baby puts a lot of extra workload on the mother's heart, kidneys, and body systems. It's totally normal for us to monitor these mums extra closely!

question: Why must nurses encourage patients with diabetes to include healthy fats in their meal plans?

options.A: Fats prevent the digestion of carbohydrates entirely.
options.B: Fats are the only nutrient that can directly lower high blood sugar.
options.C: Healthy fats protect against cardiovascular disease, a common complication of diabetes.
options.D: Unsaturated fats completely replace the need for taking daily insulin.

explanation: People with diabetes are at a much higher risk for heart problems, making heart-healthy fats an essential dietary component. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T012#GNS227_U6_T012_h2)

question: What is a major misconception regarding adolescent mental health and self-harm?

options.A: Depression in teenagers always manifests as persistent sadness and crying
options.B: Intentional injuries only occur among youths with a diagnosed psychotic disorder
options.C: Asking an adolescent directly about suicide will encourage them to try it
options.D: Cyberbullying has very little impact compared to physical fights

explanation: You got it! Asking a teen about suicide doesn't plant the idea in their head—it is a vital, caring step to assess their risk and get them immediate help.

question: If a patient takes traditional NSAIDs for a long time, which body system takes the biggest hit?

options.A: Central nervous system
options.B: Respiratory system
options.C: Reproductive system
options.D: Gastrointestinal tract

explanation: Because blocking COX-1 strips away the stomach's natural mucous defense, the GI tract is most vulnerable to long-term NSAID wear and tear. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h4)

question: Why does good teamwork improve a patient's transition from the hospital to home?

options.A: Different team members coordinate discharge education and resources smoothly
options.B: Doctors make all final decisions without consulting family members
options.C: Patients are discharged much faster without receiving any medications
options.D: Nurses take over all financial responsibilities for the household

explanation: You nailed it! Smooth teamwork ensures that when a patient is ready to go home, everyone (nurses, doctors, pharmacists, social workers) is on the same page.

question: If a patient has severe hypertension, which symptom might they complain about?

options.A: Severe pain in the lower abdomen
options.B: Morning occipital headaches
options.C: Sudden swelling in both feet
options.D: Uncontrolled trembling of hands

explanation: A pounding headache right at the back of the head (occipital area) when waking up is a classic warning sign of very high pressure. Keep storing these clinical pearls!

question: Why do old family arguments often resurface when a relative enters the terminal phase of illness?

options.A: Family members try to impress the medical staff
options.B: Hospital policies require families to argue before visiting
options.C: Medications given to the patient cause hallucinations in visitors
options.D: The approaching loss heightens emotional stress and tension

explanation: The impending death of a loved one puts intense psychological pressure on family relationships, unearthing past conflicts. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T16#GNS321_U4_T16_h4)

question: Why does blood from an upper GI bleed usually turn black and tarry (melena) by the time it comes out?

options.A: The patient has been eating too many dark green vegetables
options.B: Bile acids in the large bowel bleach the blood
options.C: Stomach bacteria turn the iron bright red
options.D: Digestive enzymes and stomach acid break down the blood during its trip

explanation: As old blood travels all the way down the long digestive tract, stomach acid and enzymes break down the hemoglobin, turning it dark, sticky, and black.

question: Which term covers both undernutrition and overnutrition?

options.A: Homeostasis
options.B: Anabolism
options.C: Metabolism
options.D: Malnutrition

explanation: Malnutrition isn't just about not having enough food—it's an umbrella term for any poor nutrition, whether someone is eating too little or too much.

question: What is the main reason behind conduction deafness?

options.A: Destruction of hair cells from loud music
options.B: Blocked transmission of sound waves to the inner ear
options.C: Damage to the auditory cortex in the brain
options.D: Degeneration of the vestibulocochlear nerve

explanation: Conduction deafness simply means a physical block—like earwax, fluid, or a stuck bone—is stopping sound waves from traveling smoothly inside.

question: What are the two main gonadotropins released by the anterior pituitary gland?

options.A: Cortisol and aldosterone
options.B: Insulin and glucagon
options.C: FSH and LH
options.D: Thyroxine and calcitonin

explanation: Spot on! Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) are the key team players secreted by the anterior pituitary.
